results.title: كييف تعلن إسقاط 124 طائرة مسيرة روسية خلال الليل
results.description: أعلن سلاح الجو الأوكراني، في بيان عبر تطبيق "تليجرام"، اليوم الخميس، أن قوات الدفاع الجوي الأوكراني أسقطت 7 طائرات مسيرة صاروخية من طراز "باندرول"، و124 من أصل 157 طائرة مسيرة، أطلقتها روسيا خلال هجوم على أوكرانيا خلال الليل. وقال البيان إن القوات الروسية شنت هجوما على أوكرانيا، خلال الليل، باستخدام صواريخ أونيكس المضادة للسفن تم إطلاقها من منطقة كورسك، وصواريخ إسكندر-إم/إس-400/كيه إن-23 الباليستية تم إطلاقها من منطقتي بريانسك وفورونيج، وأربعة صواريخ كاليبر كروز تم إطلاقها من بحر
creator: العالم

results.title: Why German business is beginning to see the UAE differently
results.description: Why German business is beginning to see the UAE differently The UAE of 2026 is not the UAE that foreign companies encountered twenty or thirty years ago. Thursday 17/09/2026 German Chancellor Friedrich Merz receives the President of the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, in Berlin, Germany, September 10, 2026. The largest number to emerge from the UAE president’s recent state visit to Germany was €40 billion, and understandably it became the headline. But while following the visit, I found myself paying more attention to something much smaller: the reaction of German business leaders after meeting Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. They did not speak only about welcoming Emirati investment into Germany. They also expressed interest in investing in the UAE and expanding cooperation with Emirati companies. I believe that change in direction deserves more attention than it has received, because money moving from the Gulf into Europe is not new. What may be changing is the way German industry itself sees the Gulf, and the UAE in particular. For much of my lifetime, the economic relationship between Europe and the Gulf was easy to understand. We bought some of the world’s best machines, vehicles, medical equipment and industrial systems from Europe, and European businesses saw this region primarily as an affluent export market. Germany occupied a particularly respected position in this equation. In the Gulf, “German engineering” was not simply a description of origin; it became shorthand for precision, durability and technical seriousness. If a machine had been designed and manufactured in Germany, the assumption was often that it had been built properly. That reputation was earned over generations. Yet precisely because this old model worked so well, it can obscure the much more interesting relationship that is now beginning to emerge. The UAE of 2026 is not the UAE that foreign companies encountered twenty or thirty years ago. The skyline is the most visible difference, but it is not the most important one. Beneath it sits an economy that increasingly wants to manufacture, develop technology, operate artificial intelligence at scale, build data infrastructure and participate in global supply chains rather than simply purchase their finished products. This does not mean that the UAE has suddenly acquired Germany’s industrial depth; it has not, and pretending otherwise would weaken rather than strengthen the argument. Germany possesses an ecosystem of engineering expertise, specialised suppliers, technical education and manufacturing knowledge that takes decades to create. What the UAE has developed is different: capital, modern infrastructure, access to energy, international connectivity and an unusual ability to move certain projects from discussion to implementation quickly. I recognise that distinction because much of my professional thinking has been shaped by operations and risk. In an operations room, having the best individual component does not necessarily produce the best system. A sophisticated technology can fail to deliver its value if the organisation around it cannot use it, maintain it or make decisions quickly enough. Conversely, a fast organisation without strong technical foundations can make the wrong decision more efficiently. The strongest systems emerge when different capabilities compensate for one another’s weaknesses. I see something similar in the relationship now developing between German industry and the UAE. Germany does not need the Emirates to become another Germany, and the Emirates should not attempt to imitate Germany’s industrial history. The opportunity is to connect what each does differently. This is why German business interest in investing inside the UAE matters. A German company that comes to the Emirates only to sell a finished product remains a supplier. A German company that establishes an engineering operation, works with an Emirati partner, develops a regional service centre, trains local specialists or adapts a technology to serve markets across the Gulf, Asia and Africa becomes part of something much larger. The UAE stops being the final destination of the product and becomes part of the system that creates, supports and distributes it. That change is subtle, but economically it is profound. The geography helps explain why this is becoming attractive. The domestic UAE market alone could never justify every investment proposition. But businesses do not necessarily have to think of the country only as a domestic market. A company operating from the UAE can look west towards Africa, east towards India and Asia, and across a Gulf region investing heavily in infrastructure, energy, healthcare, logistics and digital transformation. Ports, airports and logistics corridors matter in this calculation, but so does the ability to put engineers, customers, investors and decision-makers in the same place. For some German companies, particularly specialised industrial firms that do not possess the international footprint of a multinational corporation, the UAE can potentially become a regional operating platform rather than merely another export destination. There is a temptation in the Gulf to interpret every foreign company’s interest as proof that our economic strategy has succeeded. I would be more cautious. Corporate enthusiasm during a state visit is not the same thing as a factory, an engineering centre or a long-term investment five years later. The UAE will have to continue earning the interest it is now receiving. German companies will examine operating costs, technical talent, intellectual-property protection, energy prices, regulation and whether partnerships remain commercially viable after the ceremonies and announcements are forgotten. Serious investors should ask those questions. A strong economy should want them to. The UAE must also decide what kind of German investment it wants. A foreign company opening another sales office certainly contributes to an economy, but it is not the same as bringing engineering capability into the country. The deeper objective should be participation in knowledge. When an industrial system is installed here, can Emirati engineers understand its architecture rather than only its interface? When an artificial-intelligence platform is deployed, can local teams challenge its output and modify its assumptions, or are they permanent users of somebody else’s intelligence? When advanced manufacturing arrives, does the country acquire technicians, suppliers and research capability alongside the machinery? These questions determine whether investment creates temporary activity or lasting capability. This is one reason the German Mittelstand interests me perhaps even more than Germany’s largest corporate names. Some of the world’s most sophisticated industrial knowledge exists inside medium-sized German businesses that most ordinary consumers have never heard of. They make specialised sensors, control systems, machine tools, industrial software, pumps, precision components and technologies that sit quietly inside global manufacturing. These companies rarely generate the headlines of the largest corporations, but collectively they represent an industrial culture from which the UAE can learn enormously. At the same time, the Gulf can offer them something many of them need: a credible route into markets that are investing heavily but can be difficult to serve from Europe alone. There is another reason German business may be looking at the UAE differently, and it is connected to time. Modern technology has shortened product cycles, but the institutional process around technology has not always accelerated with it. A company can develop an excellent solution and still spend years navigating the distance between prototype, regulation, financing, customer acceptance and commercial scale. The UAE has weaknesses of its own, but one of its strongest characteristics has been a willingness to build around new sectors before every detail of the final model is known. That willingness has been visible in aviation, renewable energy, space, logistics and more recently artificial intelligence. For German companies accustomed to deep technical development, an environment willing to move quickly from discussion to pilot and from pilot to deployment can be commercially valuable. Speed, however, should never become the story by itself. The lesson the UAE can learn from Germany is that industrial strength is built through patience as well. A country can erect a factory quickly, but it cannot manufacture industrial culture at the same speed. Reliability, craftsmanship, technical education, process discipline and supplier relationships accumulate over years. One of the most valuable outcomes of a deeper UAE-Germany relationship would therefore be a productive exchange between two very different attitudes towards time: the Emirati instinct to move and the German instinct to perfect. Either one taken too far can become a weakness. Together they can become an advantage. This is why I believe the German executives’ interest in the UAE should not be treated as a courtesy accompanying a presidential visit. It may be an early sign of a larger change in how mature industrial economies perceive the Gulf. For decades, the fundamental question was what the region would buy from them. Increasingly, another question is appearing: what can they build from here, and with whom? That change would matter far beyond Germany and the Emirates. If German technology, Emirati capital and Gulf deployment capability can be combined to serve third markets, the relationship stops being purely bilateral. A technology developed in Germany may be financed with Emirati capital, tested or adapted in the UAE, supported from a regional base and eventually deployed in another country altogether. When that happens, trade has evolved into an economic network. The most successful partnership will therefore not be the one with the largest announcement. It will be the one that eventually becomes ordinary. German engineers working beside Emirati engineers; a German medium-sized company using the UAE as its regional technical centre; an Emirati investor helping a German industrial firm reach markets it could not reach alone; a technology created in one country being improved in the other and sold somewhere neither originally expected. When relationships reach that level, presidents and ministers may have opened the door, but companies and people have learned how to walk through it without being asked. That, to me, is the real significance of German business optimism about the UAE. It suggests that the Emirates may slowly be moving in the European industrial imagination from being a place where products are sold and capital originates to a place where companies themselves may want to build. The difference between those two perceptions is enormous. One describes a market. The other describes a partner.
